child_safety.score_basis: ESTIMATED -- not the exact reported figure for 'Claude Sonnet 4.6'. child_safety.notable_findings: KORA's own reporting states Claude and OpenAI's newest models lead the benchmark, with the best frontier models scoring 70-76% overall -- meaning even the safest model tested still fails or is merely adequate on roughly a quarter of tested scenarios. KORA explicitly cautions the leaderboard 'should not be interpreted as a guarantee of safety.'

environmental_impact.methodology_note: OpenAI does not publish a DALL-E 3-specific energy/CO2e/water figure. The 2.9 Wh/query and 1,594 gCO2e/1k-queries figures are not invented from nothing -- they're grounded in real, peer-reviewed-adjacent research: Luccioni, Jernite & Strubell, 'Power Hungry Processing: Watts Driving the Cost of AI Deployment?' (FAccT 2024, arXiv:2311.16863), which measured an average of ~2.9 Wh/image across tested diffusion image models and 1,594 gCO2eq per 1,000 images specifically for stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0. DALL-E 3's actual architecture and compute cost are not public, so this is an extrapolation from a comparable-class model in that study, not a DALL-E-3-specific measurement. Water is derived via OpenAI's own real water-to-energy ratio (0.000946 L/Wh, from its ChatGPT energy disclosure) applied to the 2.9 Wh figure. Green Energy Seal reflects Microsoft Azure's real 100% renewable-matching commitment (OpenAI's primary compute partner).

Meta's NLLB-200 paper (real, published) instead documents toxicity mitigation via per-language toxicity word lists and filtering of toxic training data, plus FLORES-200 human-evaluated quality benchmarks. The bias_benchmark_scores here are an approximate proxy for a real, documented equity concern in the paper: translation quality is measurably lower for the lowest-resource of the 200 languages than for high-resource ones; the exact two figures shown are estimated illustrations of that real, published disparity pattern, not exact reported numbers.

environmental_impact.methodology_note: Because this model is open-weight and commonly self-hosted, actual footprint depends on the deployer's own hardware/grid -- Meta does not publish a per-query figure for this model, and machine translation isn't one of the 10 tasks AI Energy Score measures at all. The 0.7 Wh/query estimate reflects that NLLB-200 is a 54.5B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (large total size, but likely only a few billion active parameters per token given MoE sparse routing) -- notably lower than AI Energy Score's real >66B dense 'Class C' text-generation models (0.6-3.4 Wh/query range) but higher than small dense models, consistent with typical MoE efficiency characteristics. CO2e/water are derived via the same generic constants used elsewhere in this registry (see agent/scoring.py), not measured.

ai_energy_score.disclosure: Machine translation is not one of AI Energy Score's 10 official task categories, so there is no direct benchmark analogue at all here (not just 'not measured for this model' as with the other 5 labels in this registry). The comparable_real_models above are dense large-parameter text-generation models shown only as a loose scale reference (NLLB-200 is also a large model, ~54.5B params), not a task-equivalent comparison.
